goals: Map the regional water table surface across the Naches watershed
Quantify lateral groundwater flow from hillslopes to valley aquifer
Quantify inter-column exchange fluxes (recharge vs discharge zones)
Validate mapped water table against USGS well observations
key_processes: Hillslope recharge generation (vertical infiltration and drainage)
Lateral subsurface flow from high to low elevation
Topographic control on water table depth and flow direction
drivers_to_resolve: hillslope position (recharge zones vs discharge zones)

model_choice.rationale: The question fundamentally requires 3D groundwater flow (lateral hillslope-to-valley transport and inter-column exchange), which single-column ELM cannot represent. This is a coupling problem: ELM generates distributed recharge, PFLOTRAN solves regional groundwater flow. The design below describes the ELM recharge-generation component and the required coupling architecture.
model_choice.coupling_note: ELM→PFLOTRAN one-way coupling required. ELM provides spatially-distributed sub-surface drainage (QDRAI) as top boundary recharge to a 3D PFLOTRAN domain spanning the watershed. PFLOTRAN solves steady-state or transient saturated flow to produce the regional water table surface and lateral flux fields. Without this coupling, the question is not answerable.

answerable: Distributed recharge field generation across topographic gradient (ELM can produce QDRAI at stratified hillslope/valley positions)
Local 1-D water table depth at independent points (but not as a coherent regional surface)

not_answerable.why: ELM columns are hydrologically independent — each has its own water table depth with no lateral connectivity. A regional water table surface requires 3D groundwater flow.

not_answerable.aspect: Lateral groundwater flow from hillslopes to valleys
not_answerable.why: ELM has no lateral flow physics — drainage exits the column bottom boundary and is not routed. Lateral flow requires 3D subsurface model.
not_answerable.needs: PFLOTRAN 3D saturated flow solver with ELM recharge as top BC

not_answerable.why: No inter-column communication in ELM. Exchange fluxes (hillslope recharge → valley discharge) require a coupled groundwater model.
not_answerable.needs: ELM→PFLOTRAN coupling to compute lateral flux divergence

not_answerable.aspect: Validation of regional water table against USGS wells
not_answerable.why: USGS wells measure a coherent regional water table shaped by lateral flow. ELM produces independent per-column WTD values that cannot be validated as a surface.
not_answerable.needs: Coupled model output (PFLOTRAN water table surface) for co-located well comparison

coupling_design.driver: ELM sub-surface drainage flux (QDRAI, mm/day or mm/month) at each column location → PFLOTRAN top boundary recharge flux (m³/s or m/day) at corresponding mesh nodes
coupling_design.temporal_mapping: ELM outputs monthly or annual mean QDRAI time series (1980-2018). For steady-state PFLOTRAN: use long-term mean recharge. For transient PFLOTRAN: map ELM monthly fluxes to PFLOTRAN transient top BC.
coupling_design.receiving_setup: PFLOTRAN 3D unstructured mesh spanning Naches watershed (HUC 17030002), elevation 352-1977m. Domain extends from ridgelines (no-flow lateral BC) to valley outlet (specified head or flux BC at river). Hydraulic conductivity field from regional geology/soil data. Solves saturated flow (Richards or steady-state Darcy) to produce water table surface and 3D flux field.
coupling_design.compare: Coupled (PFLOTRAN driven by ELM recharge) vs standalone ELM assumption. Standalone ELM assumes local 1-D drainage with no lateral redistribution — water table depth at each column is independent. Coupled model shows: (1) valley water tables elevated by hillslope recharge convergence, (2) hillslope water tables drawn down by lateral drainage, (3) realistic water table surface continuity, (4) quantified lateral flux from recharge to discharge zones. Validation: coupled PFLOTRAN water table vs USGS well WTD (co-located comparison, bias/RMSE). Standalone ELM cannot be validated this way.

sampling_strategy.approach: Topographically-stratified sampling to resolve recharge heterogeneity across the elevation/hillslope gradient. ELM columns placed to span hillslope positions (ridges, mid-slopes, valley bottoms) and elevation bands, generating the distributed recharge field a future PFLOTRAN run requires.

classes: ridge/upper_slope (recharge zones, steep gradient, thin soils)
valley_bottom/riparian (discharge zones, flat, deep soils, near-surface water table)

sampling_strategy.n_justification: 3 topographic positions × 3 elevation bands = 9 strata, with 2 replicates per stratum = 18 columns. This resolves the recharge gradient from ridges (high drainage) to valleys (low drainage, high water table) across the elevation/climate gradient. Replication provides uncertainty estimate on recharge rates. This is the MINIMUM to characterize distributed recharge for PFLOTRAN input.
sampling_strategy.placement_logic: Concentrate columns along elevation transects from ridges to valley bottoms, capturing the topographic flow path. Oversample valley bottoms (3-4 columns) where USGS wells exist for future validation. Use DEM-derived topographic wetness index (TWI) or slope to identify representative hillslope positions within each elevation band.
sampling_strategy.replication: 2 columns per stratum (light replication) to estimate recharge variability within each topographic-elevation class. Total 18 columns.

sampling_plan.reason: Capture snow-dominated recharge at watershed headwaters where drainage is highest and water table is deep.
Transition zone between ridge recharge and valley accumulation at high elevation.
High-elevation discharge zones where lateral flow converges and water table is shallow.
Capture mixed rain-snow recharge at ridges in the transition zone.
Dominant area of the watershed — recharge rates here control valley aquifer input.
Key discharge zones where hillslope recharge accumulates — likely location of USGS wells.
Capture rain-dominated recharge at lower watershed where drainage is lower than snow zones.
Lower watershed recharge contribution to valley aquifer.
Lowest discharge zones near watershed outlet — critical for regional water table validation.

validation_design.comparison: NOT POSSIBLE with standalone ELM. Validation requires coupled PFLOTRAN output (regional water table surface) compared to well WTD at co-located points. Standalone ELM produces independent per-column WTD that cannot represent the regional surface shaped by lateral flow.
validation_design.metric: bias, RMSE, spatial correlation (coupled PFLOTRAN water table vs well observations)
validation_design.n_validation_points: unknown — depends on USGS well density in Naches HUC 17030002. Likely 5-15 wells based on typical USGS coverage.

experiment_summary.primary_treatment: Baseline forcing (1980-2018 meteorology), native soil properties from gridded soil dataset, topographically-stratified placement. This is a RECHARGE GENERATION campaign, not a validation campaign — validation requires the coupled model.

requires_capabilities.why: To pass ELM sub-surface drainage (QDRAI) as top boundary recharge to PFLOTRAN 3D domain. This is the core missing piece — without it, the question is not answerable.
requires_capabilities.blocks: Regional water table mapping, lateral flow quantification, inter-column exchange fluxes, validation against USGS wells

requires_capabilities.capability: PFLOTRAN 3D domain setup for Naches watershed
requires_capabilities.why: Requires unstructured mesh spanning HUC 17030002 (elevation 352-1977m), hydraulic conductivity field from geology/soil data, boundary conditions (no-flow at ridges, specified head/flux at outlet).
requires_capabilities.blocks: 3D groundwater flow solution, regional water table surface output

requires_capabilities.why: To identify ridge/mid-slope/valley positions for stratified ELM column placement. Needs DEM-derived slope, TWI, or flow accumulation.
requires_capabilities.blocks: Topographically-stratified sampling (can fall back to elevation-only stratification if unavailable)

requires_capabilities.capability: USGS well data ingest and spatial indexing
requires_capabilities.why: To identify well locations within Naches HUC for future validation of coupled PFLOTRAN water table output.
requires_capabilities.blocks: Co-located validation (not critical for ELM recharge generation, but needed for coupled model validation)

requires_capabilities.capability: Gridded soil hydraulic properties (Ksat, porosity, texture) for Naches
requires_capabilities.why: ELM needs soil properties at each column location. PFLOTRAN needs 3D hydraulic conductivity field.
requires_capabilities.blocks: Realistic recharge rates (ELM) and lateral flow (PFLOTRAN)

requires_capabilities.capability: HUC boundary resolver for domain extent
requires_capabilities.why: To define Naches watershed boundary (HUC 17030002) for PFLOTRAN mesh generation and ELM column placement.
requires_capabilities.blocks: Domain definition (can use bbox as fallback, but less accurate)

assumptions: USGS well observations represent the regional water table shaped by lateral flow (not perched or local features).
Topographic position (ridge/slope/valley) is the primary control on recharge vs discharge zones — soil heterogeneity is secondary.
Long-term mean recharge (1980-2018) is sufficient for steady-state PFLOTRAN, or monthly means for transient.
ELM QDRAI (sub-surface drainage) is a reasonable proxy for groundwater recharge (ignoring deep percolation losses or lateral unsaturated flow).
PFLOTRAN domain can be meshed at resolution sufficient to resolve valley aquifer (~100m) without prohibitive computational cost.
Hydraulic conductivity field for PFLOTRAN can be derived from regional geology/soil maps (not site-specific measurements).
open_questions: What is the actual density and spatial distribution of USGS wells in Naches HUC 17030002? Are they concentrated in valleys (likely) or distributed across hillslopes?
Is transient PFLOTRAN needed (seasonal water table fluctuations) or is steady-state sufficient for the regional mapping goal?
What is the priority: build the ELM recharge generation campaign first (preparatory), or wait until ELM→PFLOTRAN coupling exists to design the full experiment?
Are there existing PFLOTRAN meshes or hydraulic conductivity datasets for the Naches region, or does this require new data preparation?
Should the design include a standalone PFLOTRAN baseline (uniform recharge) to isolate the value of spatially-distributed ELM recharge?
